Pregnancy

Preeclampsia Symptoms and Blood Pressure in Pregnancy

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Preeclampsia symptoms include high blood pressure along with a severe headache, vision changes such as spots or blurring, pain under the right ribs, sudden swelling of the face or hands, and rapid weight gain, though many people have no symptoms at all. It develops after 20 weeks of pregnancy, most often in the third trimester, and is often picked up at routine visits, which is why your blood pressure is checked every time. This guide covers the numbers clinicians use, the signs worth a same-day call, and what happens after a diagnosis, including the weeks after birth.

The blood pressure numbers that matter

In pregnancy, high blood pressure means a reading of 140/90 or higher, confirmed on two occasions at least four hours apart, starting after 20 weeks. That is the definition clinicians use for gestational hypertension. The top number is the pressure when your heart beats, the bottom number is the pressure between beats, and either one being high counts. A reading of 160/110 or higher is in the severe range. If you get a number like that at home, rest for a few minutes and check again. If it stays that high, call your care team right away: readings of 160/110 or higher that persist need to be evaluated urgently, usually in a hospital or labor and delivery unit, not at your next appointment.

One high reading is a signal, not a diagnosis. Blood pressure moves with stress, pain, caffeine, and even a rushed walk from the parking lot, which is why clinicians confirm it before labeling it. Timing matters too. High readings before 20 weeks usually point to chronic hypertension that existed before pregnancy, while new readings after 20 weeks suggest a pregnancy-related change. Preeclampsia is the next step up: high blood pressure plus protein in the urine, or signs that organs such as the liver, kidneys, or brain are under strain. That is why prenatal visits include both a cuff and a urine check.

Symptoms worth a same-day call

The symptoms that matter most are specific. A severe headache that does not ease with rest, fluids, or your usual approved pain reliever. Vision changes such as flashing lights, spots, or blurring. Pain under the right ribs or in the upper belly, which can feel like heartburn that will not settle. Sudden swelling of the face or hands, which is different from the slow ankle swelling many pregnancies bring. Rapid weight gain, such as several pounds in a few days, from fluid the body is holding. Nausea or vomiting that appears new in the second half of pregnancy. Any one of these on its own is a reason to call, not a combination requirement. Two signs skip the phone queue entirely: trouble breathing or chest pain means emergency care now, and so does a seizure, for which someone should call 911.

Just as important: preeclampsia often causes no symptoms at all, especially early on. Many people feel completely well while their blood pressure climbs, which is why every prenatal visit includes a cuff and why appointments get closer together in the third trimester. Most cases begin after 30 weeks, though preeclampsia can start any time after 20 weeks, and cases that start before 34 weeks tend to be more serious and are watched most closely. If you are around 30 weeks and notice any of the signs above, call your care team the same day rather than waiting for your next visit. Reporting a symptom that turns out to be nothing is a good outcome, not a wasted call.

Risk factors and low-dose aspirin

Some pregnancies carry a higher chance of preeclampsia. The risk is higher if you had preeclampsia before, if you have chronic high blood pressure, kidney disease, diabetes, or an autoimmune condition such as lupus, or if you are carrying twins. First pregnancies, pregnancies through IVF, a body mass index in the obese range, age 35 or older, a family history of preeclampsia, and a gap of ten years or more since a previous birth also raise the odds somewhat. Having a risk factor does not mean preeclampsia will happen. It means your care team will watch more closely and may suggest prevention.

For higher-risk pregnancies, major guidelines recommend low-dose aspirin, usually 81 mg once daily, started between about 12 and 16 weeks and continued until birth. Taken this way, it modestly lowers the chance of developing preeclampsia and of some related complications. It is one of the few preventions with solid evidence behind it, which is why clinicians bring it up early. Do not start aspirin on your own, though. The decision depends on your full history, and your clinician will confirm whether it fits your situation, along with the dose and timing. If you think your risk factors were missed at your first visits, it is reasonable to ask directly.

Checking blood pressure at home

If your care team asks you to check blood pressure at home, technique matters more than the brand of the machine. Use an upper-arm cuff that fits, since a cuff that is too small reads high. Sit quietly for about five minutes first, with your back supported, feet flat on the floor, and the cuff at heart level. Skip caffeine and exercise for half an hour beforehand, and empty your bladder. Take two readings a minute apart and record both. Checking at roughly the same times each day, such as morning and evening, gives your clinician a pattern instead of a scatter of one-off numbers.

Agree on thresholds with your care team before you start: which numbers are fine, which mean call within a day, and which mean be seen now. As a general guide, repeated readings of 140/90 or higher are worth reporting promptly, and 160/110 or higher that persists after a few minutes of rest needs urgent attention. Keep a simple log of the date, time, and both numbers. The notes in BeMama work well for this, and so does paper. Bring the log to every visit. Home readings add information between appointments, but they do not replace prenatal checks, where urine and other signs are also reviewed.

Treatment, delivery, and the weeks after birth

Delivery is the definitive treatment for preeclampsia, because the placenta drives the condition, though blood pressure can take days to weeks to settle after birth. Everything before that point is management: more frequent visits, lab tests, blood pressure medicines that are considered safe in pregnancy, and extra monitoring of the baby's growth and wellbeing. If an early birth looks likely, you may be offered steroid injections to help the baby's lungs mature, and in severe cases magnesium sulfate is given around delivery to prevent seizures. The timing of birth is a balance between how far along you are and how severe things look. Many people with milder preeclampsia are supported to around 37 weeks before delivery is recommended.

Preeclampsia can also begin after birth. Postpartum preeclampsia most often appears within the first week, but it can show up any time in the first six weeks, including in people whose blood pressure was normal for the whole pregnancy. The warning signs are the same: severe headache, vision changes, pain under the right ribs, trouble breathing, or new swelling. New parents often blame headaches on exhaustion, so be deliberate about this one. A severe headache after birth deserves a same-day call, and if it comes with vision changes or trouble breathing, emergency care. Treated promptly, postpartum preeclampsia responds well to blood pressure medicines and monitoring.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Preeclampsia is a serious blood-pressure disorder that usually develops after 20 weeks and can also occur after birth. Diagnosis depends on properly measured blood pressure and clinical assessment, not symptoms or a single home reading alone.

Severe headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, sudden swelling of the face or hands, trouble breathing, or a strong sense that something is wrong require prompt contact with maternity care.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can store readings taken with a validated device and the time symptoms began. It does not validate the cuff, diagnose preeclampsia, or decide whether a reading is safe.

When to seek help

Follow your maternity team’s thresholds. Seek urgent care for severe readings or warning symptoms, including after delivery.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • High blood pressure in pregnancy means 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks, confirmed on two checks.
  • A reading of 160/110 or higher that persists after a few minutes of rest needs urgent care right away.
  • Severe headache, vision changes, right-rib pain, or sudden face and hand swelling are call-now signs.
  • Preeclampsia is often silent, so keep every prenatal appointment even when you feel well.
  • Watch for the same warning signs for six weeks after birth, and take postpartum headaches seriously.

Frequently asked questions

What is preeclampsia?

Preeclampsia is a pregnancy condition defined by new high blood pressure after 20 weeks plus protein in the urine or signs of strain on organs such as the liver, kidneys, or brain. It affects roughly 1 in 25 pregnancies in the United States and ranges from mild to severe. It is treatable, and routine prenatal checks exist largely to catch it early.

What blood pressure is too high in pregnancy?

A reading of 140/90 or higher, confirmed on a second check at least four hours later, is considered high in pregnancy. A reading of 160/110 or higher is severely high, and if it persists after a few minutes of rest it needs urgent evaluation right away. If a home reading looks high, rest for a few minutes, recheck, and report persistent high numbers to your care team promptly.

When does preeclampsia start?

Preeclampsia starts after 20 weeks of pregnancy, most often in the third trimester, and it can also begin after birth. Cases that start before 34 weeks are less common and tend to be watched more closely. Postpartum preeclampsia usually appears within the first week after delivery but can occur up to about six weeks out.

What are the symptoms of postpartum preeclampsia?

Postpartum preeclampsia symptoms include severe headache, vision changes, pain under the right ribs, shortness of breath, new swelling, and high blood pressure readings in the first six weeks after birth. It can occur even if your blood pressure was normal during pregnancy. Treat a severe headache after delivery as a same-day medical call, and seek emergency care if vision changes or breathing trouble come with it.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
